facts.F1: The Plaintiff bought into a promotion run by United Airlines, which awarded a one-carat diamond ring as the first prize to the winner of a draw
facts.F2: The promotion required the winner to fill out a coupon, with the winner being the person whose name was on the coupon
facts.F3: The 1st Defendant company distributed coupons to the Plaintiff and the 3rd Defendant, who were employees of the company, to fill out in their names

facts.F1: Television Broadcasts Limited (TVB), a company listed on the Main Board of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, announced an offer to repurchase up to 120 million of its shares at HK$35.075 per share for a total consideration of up to HK$4,209 million
facts.F2: TVB's largest shareholder and parties regarded as acting in concert with it (Concert Group) have an aggregate 29.9% stake in the company and intend not to take up the Offer in respect of any of their shares
facts.F3: The Concert Group has 4 representatives sitting on TVB's board as non-executive directors, and the increase in their holding in TVB in consequence of TVB's buy-back of its own shares would be treated as an acquisition of voting rights for the purposes of the Codes on Takeovers and Mergers and Share Buy-backs issued by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC)
facts.F4: The Offer is made subject to the passing of an ordinary resolution to approve the whitewash waiver by the independent shareholders of TVB at the EGM
facts.F5: The Broadcasting Ordinance (BO) prescribes a special regime of controls over domestic free television licensees, including a scale-back provision (s 19 of Schedule 1) that caps the votes of non-Hong Kong resident shareholders at any general meeting at 49%
facts.F6: TVB's second largest shareholder, Silchester International Investors LLP, is a London-based investment fund holding a stake of over 14% and is an unqualified voting controller subject to the scale-back provision
facts.F7: The scale-back provision in s 19 of Schedule 1 to the Broadcasting Ordinance has overriding effect and applies to any question or matter determined by a poll at a general meeting of the licensee

claim: The applicant claims that the Commissioner of Transport acted beyond his powers conferred by the legislation by prioritising 'committed vacancies' over the applicant's clean applications, and seeks a declaration that he is entitled to have his applications entertained.

facts.F1: The applicant, TSE Kai-chow, is the managing partner of the Leung Chow Public Car Co. and had ambitions to run a fleet of 200 public light buses.
facts.F2: He submitted applications for registration of 25 public light buses in July 1976, which were refused by the Commissioner of Transport due to a Gazette notice limiting the number of registrable public light buses to 4,350.
facts.F3: The applicant's original contention was that he was entitled to have his applications considered without regard to 'committed vacancies'.
facts.F4: The Commissioner had made commitments to register vehicles belonging to other persons, who had not yet submitted their applications, prior to the applicant's applications.
facts.F5: The applicant concedes that the 25 vehicles originally applied for have since been disposed of, but seeks a declaration that if he makes new applications for 4 similar vehicles, the Commissioner ought to entertain them without regard to prior commitments.
facts.F6: The Commissioner opposes the application, citing public safety and the need to regulate vehicular traffic, and also raises technical objections to the applicant's original applications.
facts.F7: The Commissioner's departmental policy, which involves giving assurances to certain persons that their applications are likely to succeed, is not provided for by the law.
facts.F8: The legislation is addressed to the public generally and gives no selective protection to the interests of any particular segment thereof.

reference_issues: Whether the Commissioner of Transport acted beyond his powers conferred by the legislation by prioritising 'committed vacancies' over the applicant's clean applications.
Whether the departmental policy of giving assurances to certain persons that their applications are likely to succeed is valid and binding.
Whether the applicant's original applications were technically imperfect and therefore not entitled to be considered.

facts.F5: The applicants’ claims were made on the basis that, if refouled, they would be harmed or killed by the 1st applicant’s husband Dede and the loan shark.
facts.F6: According to the 1st applicant, in around 2006, she borrowed some money from the loan shark for her family’s financial hardship after the birth of her daughter.
facts.F7: She and Dede undertook for the repayments but she later found that Dede had an affair. When she confronted him, Dede hit her and the applicant left for her mother’s house for refuge.
facts.F8: Dede begged her for reunion and, upon her refusal, Dede vandalized her family home. Thereafter, the first applicant went to work overseas. From then on, Dede had been harassing her and threatening her for the remittance of money to pay off his loan shark.
facts.F9: He also threatened to kill the 2nd applicant who was born out of wedlock. Out of fear, she stayed in Hong Kong for protection.
facts.F10: The Director assessed the applicants’ claims as a composite claim and refused the applicants’ claims on all applicable grounds.
facts.F11: The Director found that the level of risk of harm from Dede and the loan sharks upon the applicants’ refoulement was assessed to be low.
facts.F12: State protection was available to them and internal relocation was an option open to them.

facts.F17: In any event, state protection and internal relocation were both available to them. For these reasons, the Board rejected the applicants’ claims on all applicable grounds and dismissed their appeal.
facts.F18: The Director and the Board had both treated the applicants’ claim as a composite claim.

Defendant: (1)The Chief Executive, (2) The Secretary for the Civil Service

facts.F1: The Chief Executive promulgated two instruments, the Public Service (Administration) Order 1997 (E.O. No. 1 of 1997) (the Executive Order) and the Public Service (Disciplinary) Regulation (the Regulation), which were intended to replace the provisions relating to the topics in the Letters Patent and the Colonial Regulations that lapsed on 30th June 1997.
facts.F2: The decisions of the Secretary for the Civil Service, which were contained in a memorandum circulated on 12th July 1997, announced revised arrangements for overseas officers who transfer to local conditions of service.
facts.F3: One of those decisions has been overtaken by events, leaving only one decision, contained in para. 3(e) of the memorandum, to be challenged, which stated that a transferee will cease to be eligible for sea passage, homeward passage and baggage allowance on finally leaving the service.
facts.F4: This decision was challenged on the ground that it abrogates accrued contractual rights.
facts.F5: The court applied the test laid down by Godfrey J. (as he then was) in the Court of Appeal in R. v. Director of Immigration ex p. Ho Ming Sai (1993) 3 HKPLR 157 at p.170 to determine whether a particular point is arguable.

reference_issues: Whether the two instruments promulgated by the Chief Executive are lawful and do not contravene Article 48(7) of the Basic Law
Whether the decisions of the Secretary for the Civil Service, as contained in the memorandum, are lawful
Whether the Association of Expatriate Civil Servants of Hong Kong has standing to challenge the decisions
Whether certain provisions in the Executive Order and the Regulation are incompatible with the Bill of Rights and other laws

claim: claims for breach of contract and constructive trust against the defendant
requested_remedy: claims for breach of contract and constructive trust against the defendant

facts.F1: The defendant, Mr. Chau, was the controlling owner of New Nongkai, which acquired 75% shares in Shanghai Land Holdings Limited.
facts.F2: In May 2003, US$39 million was taken out of the plaintiff's bank account with the Bank of China at Mr. Chau's request.
facts.F3: The money was transferred to various entities, including Fuyou Securities Brokerage Co. Ltd. and Shanghai Mechanics International Trading Limited.
facts.F4: The plaintiff alleges that the money was misappropriated by Mr. Chau for improper purposes.
facts.F5: The defendant was arrested in Shanghai in May 2003 and was subsequently tried and jailed.
facts.F6: The plaintiff's receivers were appointed by the court in June 2003 to manage the company's affairs.
facts.F7: The defendant's ordinary residence is in Hong Kong, not Shanghai.

reference_issues: Whether the court has jurisdiction to hear the claim against the defendant, who is outside the jurisdiction.
Whether the plaintiff has a good arguable case under Order 11(1)(a), (d), (e), and (p).
Whether the Labour Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction over the employment contract claim.
Whether the defendant has submitted to the jurisdiction of the court.

requested_remedy: Leave to apply for judicial review to challenge the Listing Review Committee’s decision to uphold the decision to cancel the listing of Blockchain Group Company Limited (in liquidation) under Rule 6.01A of the Rules Governing the Listing of Securities on The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited
parties: Defendant: The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited

facts.F1: The Applicant is a shareholder holding (directly and indirectly) an aggregate of 25.13% of Blockchain Group Company Limited’s shares.
facts.F2: The Company was wound up by order of Anthony Chan J made on 19 November 2018, and its shares were suspended from trading on the same day.
facts.F3: By the Listing Committee Decision dated 12 June 2020, the Company’s listing under Rule 6.01A was cancelled on grounds of failure to meet the resumption conditions and non-existence of exceptional circumstances justifying extension.
facts.F4: The LRC upheld the Listing Committee’s decision on 16 November 2020, citing that the Company had failed to meet the resumption conditions even by the date of the LRC hearing and there were no exceptional circumstances justifying an extension of the remedial period.
facts.F5: The Applicant seeks to challenge the LRC Decision, citing lack of independence and impartiality of the LRC, inadequate reasons, and failure to consider relevant matters.
facts.F6: The Listing Rules impose requirements on listed companies and their directors to ensure that investors have and can maintain confidence in the market.
facts.F7: The SFO requires the Exchange to ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, an orderly, informed and fair market.
facts.F8: The Exchange operates the stock market in Hong Kong and acts as the frontline regulator of listed companies and their directors.
facts.F9: The Listing Committee has reserved to itself the power to cancel the listing of a listed issuer and is the first instance decision-maker in respect of all cancellation decisions.
facts.F10: The Listing Committee made the decision to cancel the listing on 12 June 2020.

reference_issues: Whether the Applicant has standing to bring the application for leave to apply for judicial review.
Whether the listing review committee (LRC) has independence and impartiality under Article 10 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance Cap 383.
Whether the grounds for review are reasonably arguable.
Whether the Applicant has succeeded in demonstrating a basis to impugn the LRC’s decision.

claim: The applicant seeks leave to launch judicial review proceedings to challenge the decision of the Transport Tribunal made on 31 July 2008.
requested_remedy: The applicant seeks leave to launch judicial review proceedings to challenge the decision of the Transport Tribunal made on 31 July 2008.
parties: Plaintiff: MAN YEE TRANSPORT BUS CO LTD
Defendant: TRANSPORT TRIBUNAL, COMMISSIONER FOR TRANSPORT

facts.F1: The Transport Tribunal made a decision on 31 July 2008, confirming the Commissioner for Transport's decision to cancel the passenger service licences of the applicant in respect of two buses bearing registration marks GV6278 and LF4793, but varied the decision to suspension for a period of 48 months for LF4793.
facts.F2: The applicant and its associated company, Nam Kee, are bus operators of different bus routes.
facts.F3: On 6 and 21 September 2006, the applicant deployed GV6278 and LF4793, which were owned by the applicant and licensed to run on other routes, to provide services from Johnston Road in Wanchai to Tuen Mun.
facts.F4: The applicant acted in breach of the relevant conditions in the passenger service licences in respect of the two buses, the licensing conditions for a non-franchised bus and the relevant provisions in the Road Traffic Ordinance (Cap 374).
facts.F5: The applicant does not dispute that it has acted in breach of the relevant conditions and provisions in the Road Traffic Ordinance but argues that the punishment imposed is too severe.
facts.F6: The applicant contends that the Transport Tribunal has come to wrong findings of fact regarding the deployment of GV6278 and LF4793 on route no. NR719.
facts.F7: The Transport Tribunal found that the applicant was using the two buses to carry out Mun Mo operations on the dates in question.
facts.F8: The applicant complains that the Transport Tribunal wrongly refused to allow the applicant to adduce evidence to show that some buses of Nam Kee running on the route in question were under repair on the dates in question.
facts.F9: There was quite sufficient evidence before the Tribunal to justify its findings or inferences of fact.
facts.F10: The applicant had received warning letters from the Commissioner for similar breaches after the change of ownership and management.

reference_issues: Whether the Transport Tribunal's findings of fact regarding the deployment of GV6278 and LF4793 on route no. NR719 were justified.
Whether the punishment imposed by the Transport Tribunal was excessive.
Whether the Transport Tribunal should have taken into account previous similar breaches by the applicant when it was under a different ownership and management.
authorities: Road Traffic Ordinance (Cap 374)
